source.title: Gaussian process surrogate models for neural networks
source.authors: Michael Y. Li; Erin Grant; T. Griffiths

record.file_problem: none; the supplied text includes the paper and supplementary material.
record.tranche_reason: The paper measures whether properties learned from trained neural networks predict their generalization gap, using kernel lengthscale correlations and GP marginal likelihood. These are different measures from the properties named in V1–V8.
record.gate_note: The study's own generalization-gap results bear on the broad claim about measured properties tracking generalization, but do not test any of V1–V8 as specified. The paper also reports spectral-bias, depth-pathology, and influence-estimation results; those do not test the listed claim versions. Cited prior-work results are not recorded as rows.
record.test_reason: The study predicts regression-network generalization using GP surrogate lengthscales and marginal likelihood. It does not test V1–V8: these predictors are not magnitude-aware sharpness, its influence analysis does not measure test-accuracy loss after removing memorized examples, and its synthetic optimizer comparisons do not test V4's benchmark and tuning conditions.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate for the generalization experiments. The authors conclude more broadly that empirically learned GP surrogates can capture spectral bias and depth pathologies, identify influential points, and predict generalization. They present this as a promising empirical framework, with the current evidence restricted to feed-forward networks and regression tasks.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses learned GP surrogate kernels to predict generalization behavior in regression networks; it does not reproduce the methods or settings of the claim versions.
record.method_sensitivity: In the larger sweep, the lengthscale-correlation relationship varies by dataset: it is positive for pendulum and negative for most others. The marginal-likelihood relationship is reported as sensitive to jitter, set to 0.5 in the analysis.

fits_no_version.finding: Data–surrogate lengthscale similarity negatively correlates with generalization gap across the initial UCI experiments; the larger sweep shows dataset-dependent exceptions.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Similarity between data and GP-surrogate lengthscale profiles can track regression-network generalization gaps, with dataset and surrogate-fit dependence.

fits_no_version.finding: Surrogate marginal likelihood negatively correlates with test error in five of seven selected UCI datasets and ranks sine versus ReLU families in synthetic experiments.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: GP-surrogate marginal likelihood can predict relative regression-network test performance in some settings, subject to dataset and jitter sensitivity.

record.peer_reviewed: Conference on Uncertainty in Artificial Intelligence (UAI 2023)
record.problems: The experiments are restricted to feed-forward networks and regression tasks. The larger UCI sweep has exceptions, and the marginal-likelihood relationship is sensitive to jitter. Several exact plotted values and uncertainty estimates are not stated in the text.
record.rows_left_out: The paper also reports spectral-bias, depth-pathology, and influence-estimation results in Sections 4.1–4.3, plus supplementary marginal-likelihood comparisons in Sections A.1.1–A.1.2. These do not measure the claim versions or add a distinct generalization-gap result required for this catalog entry.

untested.parts: Random-label fitting, natural-label held-out accuracy, and chance performance with random labels.
Test-error behavior as width increases beyond the width required for zero training error.
Convolutional versus fully connected image classifiers and the contribution of local connectivity.
Adaptive versus SGD generalization on image and language benchmarks under the specified tuning regimes and remedies.
Batch-size effects under fixed epoch budgets and recipe adaptations that remove the penalty.
Dropout effects on held-out error, including training-set size, excessive dropout, and data augmentation.
Magnitude-aware weight-perturbation sharpness, its association with generalization gaps, and comparisons with norm and margin measures.
Test accuracy after removing highly memorized examples versus equally many random examples.

record.verdict_notes: No verdicts apply to V1–V8. The corrected row states indicate that these measures cannot determine the listed versions, not that the study's reported surrogate relationships are absent.

versions.untested_parts: Random-label memorization and natural-label generalization coexistence.
Test error as width increases beyond interpolation.
Convolutional versus fully connected image-classification generalization.
Adaptive optimizers versus SGD held-out performance.
Large-batch generalization under fixed epoch budgets.
Magnitude-aware sharpness and its comparison with norm- and margin-based measures.
Effects of removing memorized training examples on test accuracy.

rows.subject: ensembles of randomly initialized NNs with SiLU, GELU, ReLU, or tanh activations
rows.size_stated: 25 NNs per ensemble; two layers of 128 hidden units
rows.operation_detail: Correlated the data and surrogate kernel lengthscale profiles across features with the generalization gap across UCI datasets.
rows.measure: Spearman correlation (ρ) and Pearson correlation (r) between lengthscale-profile correlation and generalization gap
rows.value: Across architectures and maximum training iterations, ρ ranges from −0.868 to −0.716 and r ranges from −0.856 to −0.528.
rows.uncertainty: Mean generalization gap with standard error is reported; exact errors are shown in Figure 7 only.
rows.note: The authors report the aggregate ranges across the tested activation, step-count, and dataset conditions; separate plotted values are not transcribed.
rows.check: The reported correlation ranges agree with Figure 7, but lengthscale-profile similarity does not measure any listed version. Training stops at the iteration limit or zero training error; the stated step counts are maximum budgets.

rows.subject: neural network ensembles with four activations, two depths, two widths, and two Adam learning rates
rows.size_stated: 50 NNs per ensemble; widths 32 or 64; depths 2 or 4
rows.operation_detail: Compared lengthscale-profile correlation with generalization gap across neural-network hyperparameter combinations and UCI datasets.

conditions.value: 500 iterations; full-batch Adam; learning rates 0.03 or 0.003

rows.measure: Correlation between lengthscale-profile correlation and generalization gap
rows.value: A negative relationship is reported in 5/7 datasets; pendulum has ρ = 0.54 and r = 0.50; protein has ρ = −0.39 and r = −0.34.
rows.uncertainty: Mean generalization gap and standard error are plotted; exact errors are not stated in text.
rows.note: The aggregate result and the two named exceptions are reported in text. Figure 8 shows the other dataset-specific coefficients.
rows.check: This measures a different generalization predictor. The protein coefficients are misassigned: Figure 8 gives protein ρ = −0.05 and r = 0.19; ρ = −0.39 and r = −0.34 belong to autompg. Pendulum has ρ = 0.54 and r = 0.50. The prose calls protein a positive exception, although its plotted Spearman coefficient is slightly negative.

rows.subject: neural network ensembles with four activations, two depths, two widths, and two Adam learning rates
rows.size_stated: 50 NNs per ensemble; widths 32 or 64; depths 2 or 4
rows.operation_detail: Compared test error with training-data marginal likelihood under the surrogate kernel learned for each network family.
rows.measure: Correlation between marginal likelihood and test error
rows.value: A larger marginal likelihood correlates with lower test error in 5/7 datasets.
rows.note: The text says this result is sensitive to jitter; the reported analysis uses jitter 0.5. Dataset-specific coefficients are shown in Figure 9.
rows.check: The 5/7 aggregate agrees with Figure 9, but surrogate marginal likelihood does not measure any listed version. The result uses jitter 0.5 and is explicitly sensitive to that choice.

rows.subject: neural network ensembles with sine or ReLU activations, one or three hidden layers
rows.size_stated: 50 NNs per family; 256 hidden units per layer
rows.stage_stated: trained with vanilla full-batch gradient descent or Adam
rows.operation_detail: Compared test error with marginal likelihood under a GP surrogate across architectures and learning algorithms.

conditions.value: one or three hidden layers; 256 units
0.01 for vanilla gradient descent; 0.003 or 0.0003 for Adam

rows.measure: Test MSE and marginal likelihood of training data under surrogate
rows.value: Across architectures and learning algorithms, the NN family whose surrogate assigns higher marginal likelihood achieves lower test error.
rows.uncertainty: Mean and standard error of test MSE are plotted; exact errors are not stated in text.
rows.note: The reported relationship concerns comparisons between sine and ReLU NN families on the stated target.
rows.check: Figure 12 supports ranking sine versus ReLU families within the tested depth and optimizer conditions. It does not establish that Adam generalizes worse than SGD under V4's benchmark and tuning conditions. Surrogate kernels here are learned from randomly initialized networks, rather than trained-network predictions.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.
